metadata.title: Andean crops nutrient composition dataset
metadata.description: Proximate composition, energy and selected minerals of eight Andean crops, with per-value provenance and verification status.
metadata.basis: All values are per 100 g edible portion of the food in the state described for each crop (dry seed or kernel, dried hypocotyl or fresh tuber). Values are not comparable across these states without conversion.

verification_levels.verified: Checked against the primary source record by a curator.
verification_levels.corroborated: Matches the named source record as reproduced by at least one independent secondary copy; the primary record was not accessed.
verification_levels.unverified: Source not identified, or value not checked against any source.

methods.text: Values are expressed per 100 g edible portion of the food as described. Dry-matter values are calculated as value × 100 / (100 − water) and are shown only where water content is available. Per-energy values are calculated as value × 100 / energy and express nutrient density per 100 kcal.
Each record states whether the source food matches the crop directly or is a proxy (for example, a source that does not specify the species).

Energy is recalculated with general conversion factors of 4 kcal/g for protein and available carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g for fat and 2 kcal/g for dietary fibre, approximating available carbohydrate as total carbohydrate by difference minus dietary fibre. A difference of more than 10 % from the reported energy is flagged for review. The 10 % tolerance is a screening heuristic set for this dataset, not a published limit.

Where water and ash are reported, the sum of water, protein, fat, total carbohydrate and ash is expected to lie between 97 and 103 g/100 g. When carbohydrate is calculated by difference the sum equals 100 g by construction, so this check mainly detects transcription errors and values combined from different samples.

components.label: Energy
components.description: Metabolisable energy as reported by the source.

components.label: Protein
components.description: Total protein, conventionally calculated from total nitrogen; the nitrogen conversion factor is not recorded.

components.label: Fat, total
components.description: Total lipid. INFOODS distinguishes fat tagnames by analytical method; the method is not recorded here.

components.label: Carbohydrate, total (by difference)
components.description: Total carbohydrate calculated by difference; includes dietary fibre. It is not available carbohydrate.

components.label: Dietary fibre
components.description: Total dietary fibre for USDA-sourced values. For undocumented sources the method is unknown and the value may be crude fibre (INFOODS FIBC), which is not comparable with total dietary fibre.

components.label: Iron
components.description: Total iron; bioavailability is not represented.

sources.title: Glucosinolate survey of cultivated and feral mashua (Tropaeolum tuberosum Ruíz & Pavón) in the Cuzco region of Peru

Antioxidant capacity and secondary metabolites in four species of Andean tuber crops: native potato (Solanum sp.), mashua (Tropaeolum tuberosum Ruiz & Pavón), oca (Oxalis tuberosa Molina) and ulluco (Ullucus tuberosus Caldas)
sources.container: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture

water.note: Corroborated by scaling a per-cup (170 g) listing of the source record to 100 g.

ash.note: Corroborated by scaling a per-cup (170 g) listing of the source record to 100 g.

notes.text: Flavonoids, chiefly quercetin and kaempferol glycosides; total flavonoids in the quinoa and kañiwa samples studied ranged from 36.2 to 144.3 mg/100 g.
Bitter saponins are concentrated in the outer seed layers; grain is usually dehulled or polished and washed before use, and low-saponin ('sweet') cultivars are being developed.
Seed oil with linoleic acid as the main fatty acid and a high tocopherol content (reported jointly for quinoa and kañiwa).

image.alt: Close-up of white quinoa grains

food.description: Amaranth grain, uncooked (species not specified by the source)
food.note: Water and ash were not added because they could not be corroborated for this source record; dry-matter values are therefore unavailable.

composition.source_record: FDC ID 170682 (SR Legacy NDB 20001), 'Amaranth grain, uncooked'

notes.text: No quantifiable flavonoids were found in the kiwicha samples studied, in contrast to quinoa and kañiwa.
Amaranth seed oil contains squalene; one study reported 4.2 % squalene in crude Amaranthus oil.

flags.text: Composition values describe amaranth grain of unspecified species and are used as a proxy for Amaranthus caudatus.

notes.text: Flavonoids, chiefly quercetin and isorhamnetin glycosides.
Seed oil with linoleic acid as the main fatty acid and a high tocopherol content (reported jointly for quinoa and kañiwa).

food.note: Debittered, cooked tarwi as eaten has a much higher water content than the dry seed.

notes.text: Raw seeds contain bitter, toxic quinolizidine alkaloids (mainly lupanine, with sparteine and hydroxylupanines) and are debittered before consumption, traditionally by soaking, cooking and repeated washing in water.
Lipid fraction dominated by oleic acid (monounsaturated) and linoleic acid (polyunsaturated).

flags.text: The raw seed is not eaten; values do not describe the debittered food as consumed.

image.alt: Tarwi seeds (Lupinus mutabilis)

taxon.note: Some authors treat cultivated maca as Lepidium peruvianum.

food.description: Hypocotyl, dried (inferred from energy density; not documented by a source)

notes.text: Cultivated in the central Andes of Peru at about 4000–4500 m altitude.
Macamides (N-benzylalkamides) and macaenes; macamides are reported to form mainly during post-harvest drying.
Clinical evidence for the health effects attributed to maca is limited.

flags.text: Energy, carbohydrate, calcium and iron coincide with values declared on at least one commercial maca-powder label (rounded label declarations, not analytical data). The origin of the other values is unknown, so the record may combine values from different products or samples.

image.alt: Maca hypocotyls with leaves

taxon.note: Purple-pigmented Andean maize. Version 0.1 used the informal name 'Zea mays amylacea', which is not used here.

food.description: Kernel, dry (not documented by a source)

notes.text: Anthocyanins (cyanidin-3-glucoside, pelargonidin-3-glucoside and peonidin-3-glucoside, with acylated forms), together with p-coumaric and ferulic acids and quercetin derivatives.
Reported health effects of purple-corn phenolics come mainly from cell and animal studies; evidence from human studies is limited.

image.alt: Purple maize cob (maíz morado), museum specimen

food.description: Tuber, fresh (inferred from energy density; not documented by a source)

notes.text: Three aromatic glucosinolates identified; total contents ranged from 0.27 to 50.74 µmol/g dried tuber and were highest in feral plants.
Highest antioxidant capacity and phenolic, anthocyanin and carotenoid contents of the four Andean tuber crops compared (native potato, mashua, oca and ulluco).

image.alt: Mashua tubers of several colours from Peru

food.description: Tuber, fresh (inferred from energy density; not documented by a source)

notes.text: Contains oxalate; contents vary between cultivars and are reported to fall during traditional post-harvest exposure to sunlight, which also raises sugar content.
Analysed for antioxidant capacity, phenolics, anthocyanins and carotenoids alongside native potato, mashua and ulluco; mashua had the highest values.
